neighbours.label: archaic possessive 'hath'/'hast' (Early Modern English 'have'), peaking on 'hath' or the object article right after it
fire: In the old tale the miller hath a daughter fairer than any queen.
Quoth the knight, thou hast a brave heart for one so young.
Verily the king hath a hundred horses in his stable.
And the shepherd said, the wolf hath a cunning mind.
Good sir, thou hast a strange look upon thy face this morn.
The poet wrote that the moon hath a silver crown at night.
My lord, this castle hath a secret door beneath the stair.
Then spake the friar: thou hast a debt that must be paid.
quiet: In the old tale the miller has a daughter fairer than any queen.
The coach told him he has a brave heart for one so young.
Apparently the king owns a hundred horses in his stable.
And the shepherd said that the wolf is a cunning creature.
Good grief, you have a strange look on your face this morning.
The poet wrote that the moon wears a silver crown at night.
My friend, this castle contains a secret door beneath the stair.
Then the banker said: you owe a debt that must be paid.

notes: Top examples mix modern main-verb have/has/had with archaic 'hath a'/'hast a'; probing showed modern have/has scores low (<0.2) while hath/hast + object reached 0.4-0.8. Near misses swap in modern has/have.
